body:
What is Maru-Gurjara architecture?

Maru-Gurjara architecture is a distinctive regional tradition of Indian temple and monumental architecture that developed in western India, particularly in present-day Gujarat and Rajasthan. It reached a highly developed form during the medieval period, especially from the 11th to the 13th centuries CE.

The name combines geographical and cultural associations. Maru refers to the Rajasthan region, while Gurjara refers to the historical Gujarat region. The term is used to identify a tradition shaped by the interaction of architectural practices in these adjoining areas.

The same tradition is frequently called Solanki architecture because it flourished under the Chaulukya rulers of Gujarat, commonly known as the Solankis. However, the 2 expressions are not exactly identical in scope. Solanki architecture emphasises the historical period and dynastic patronage, whereas Maru-Gurjara refers to the architectural tradition, which also appeared outside Solanki political territory and continued after the dynasty's principal period of power.

Maru-Gurjara architecture is a western Indian regional development of the Nagara tradition, distinguished by carefully articulated temple plans, projecting and recessed walls, elaborate stone carving, richly decorated pillars, ornamental entrances and intricately carved ceilings.

The Solanki or Chaulukya rulers of Gujarat

The Chaulukyas established a major medieval kingdom in Gujarat, with Anahilapataka or Anhilwad Patan as their capital. Their rule provided an important setting for the expansion of temple construction, reservoirs, stepwells and other architectural projects.

Among the rulers particularly associated with this architectural heritage were Bhima I, Siddharaja Jayasimha and Kumarapala. Royal patronage was not the only source of construction. Queens, ministers, merchants, religious communities and other donors also financed significant monuments.

This explains why the surviving heritage includes both Hindu and Jain temples, as well as water structures intended for public use. The same regional craftsmanship could serve different religious and social purposes.

Relationship with Nagara temple architecture

Indian temple architecture is commonly introduced through the broad Nagara tradition of northern India and the Dravida tradition of southern India. These broad categories include numerous regional variations.

Maru-Gurjara architecture belongs principally to the Nagara family. Like other Nagara temples, its principal shrine commonly has a tower known as a shikhara above the sanctum. The tower generally rises in a curving or progressively inward-tapering form. In contrast, the typical Dravida temple has a tiered pyramidal vimana above the sanctum and may feature large entrance towers called gopurams.

The distinctive identity of a Maru-Gurjara temple therefore lies not simply in the presence of a shikhara but in the combination of its plan, wall treatment, pillared halls, ceiling design and sculptural decoration.

Why Gujarat became an important architectural centre

Medieval Gujarat contained royal centres, pilgrimage places, markets and skilled craft communities. Rulers and prosperous donors supported monuments that expressed religious devotion, political prestige and public welfare.

Stone architecture depended on cooperation between architects, masons, sculptors and other craftspeople. The development of richly ornamented buildings also drew upon the region's established traditions of woodcarving and decorative design.

Religious structures and waterworks became closely connected. A temple might stand beside a stepped reservoir, while a stepwell could itself receive elaborate architectural and sculptural treatment. This relationship is especially important at Modhera and Rani-ki-Vav.

Prelims focus

  • Maru-Gurjara architecture developed principally in Gujarat and Rajasthan.
  • It is a regional development of Nagara temple architecture.
  • The Chaulukyas of Gujarat are commonly called the Solankis.
  • Anhilwad Patan was an important Solanki capital.
  • Its principal period of development was the medieval era, especially the 11th–13th centuries CE.
  • Trap: Maru-Gurjara is not exclusively a Jain style, nor is every monument built in this style necessarily a Solanki royal commission.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 69–76 and 94–95; Krishna Deva, Temples of North India, National Book Trust, 1969, chapters V–VI, printed pp. 38–48; M. A. Dhaky, The Genesis and Development of Maru-Gurjara Temple Architecture, in Studies in Indian Temple Architecture, 1975, pp. 146–161; Patan District Administration, History, consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Maru-Gurjara Architecture: Origins, Region and Historical Background

body:
The basic arrangement of the temple

A Solanki temple follows the fundamental organisation of a North Indian temple but often develops it into a carefully planned sequence of interconnected spaces.

The innermost chamber is the garbhagriha, or sanctum, which houses the principal sacred image. Worshippers approach it through one or more halls and entrance spaces. The most characteristic architectural terms are explained below.

Architectural elementMeaning and function
GarbhagrihaInner sanctum containing the principal sacred image.
GudhamandapaEnclosed or relatively closed pillared hall adjoining the sanctum.
SabhamandapaAssembly hall; in major Solanki complexes it may be a separate, open-sided pillared structure.
ArdhamandapaEntrance porch or smaller transitional hall.
ToranaOrnamented ceremonial entrance or arch-like gateway.
ShikharaSuperstructure rising above the sanctum.
AmalakaRibbed, disc-like crowning element on many Nagara towers.
KalashaPot-shaped finial crowning the tower.

Not every Solanki temple contains every element in the same arrangement. Smaller shrines may have only a sanctum, hall and porch, whereas larger establishments may include a separate assembly hall, subsidiary shrines and monumental gateways.

Plan and elevation

The plan describes the arrangement of spaces as viewed from above. The elevation describes the vertical form of the building, including its base, walls, roof and tower.

A typical substantial Solanki temple links the sanctum with an enclosed hall and entrance porch. Larger examples may place a separate assembly hall and an ornamental torana along the same principal axis. Modhera offers a particularly clear example of this arrangement.

Characteristic treatment of walls and towers

One of the recognisable features of developed Maru-Gurjara architecture is the multiplication of projections and recesses in exterior walls. Instead of presenting one flat surface, the wall repeatedly advances and retreats. Sculptured niches and ornamental bands occupy these surfaces.

This arrangement gives the building a strong rhythm of light and shadow. Some temple towers also contain clusters of smaller tower-like forms around the main shikhara. Their presence makes the vertical composition more elaborate, although the precise design varies between monuments.

The latina or rekha-prasada is a common Nagara tower form with a curving outline. A phamsana roof, by contrast, is generally broader, lower and composed of sloping tiers. In northern Indian temple architecture, phamsana forms are often associated with halls rather than the principal sanctum tower.

A shikhara is the tower above the main sanctum. A mandapa is a hall. A torana is an ornamental entrance. These are different architectural elements and should not be treated as interchangeable terms.

The distinctive interior

Solanki temple interiors are especially noted for their elaborately sculpted pillars and ceilings. In major halls, pillars may form an octagonal arrangement, supporting stone beams and a central ceiling.

The ceiling can be built from successive concentric rings of carved stone that become progressively smaller towards the centre. A richly sculpted central pendant, often resembling a hanging lotus or ornamental cluster, completes the composition.

Carved brackets, decorative arches between pillars, foliage, geometric designs and sculpted figures add to the visual richness. Such carving is particularly prominent in the Jain marble temples at Mount Abu and Kumbhariya.

Construction and craftsmanship

Many of these buildings relied extensively on the trabeate or post-and-lintel system: horizontal stone beams carried by vertical columns. Corbelling was another important technique. In corbelled construction, successive stone courses project inward until they meet or support a covering element. This principle helps explain the construction of elaborate stone ceilings.

A carved torana may look like an arch, but its visual shape alone does not establish that it works as a true structural arch. A true arch transfers loads through wedge-shaped units and their lateral thrust, whereas corbelled construction relies on overlapping horizontal courses. The distinction matters when comparing medieval Indian buildings.

Stone surfaces also preserve features reminiscent of Gujarat's woodcarving tradition. The similarity lies in the ornamental language and carved detailing; it does not mean that all stone architectural forms were physically constructed like wooden buildings.

Prelims focus

  • Garbhagriha: inner sanctum.
  • Gudhamandapa: enclosed hall; sabhamandapa: assembly hall.
  • Torana: ornamental gateway.
  • Latina or rekha-prasada: curving Nagara shikhara form.
  • Developed Solanki interiors frequently feature richly carved pillars, octagonal arrangements and concentric ceiling rings.
  • Trap: An ornamental arch-shaped torana is not necessarily a true load-bearing arch.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 6, printed pp. 69–76; NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings, printed pp. 61–63; Krishna Deva, Temples of North India, 1969, chapter VI, printed pp. 45–47.]

pictures.alt: A representative Solanki temple sequence links porch, enclosed hall and sanctum, with a tower above the sanctum and optional separate hall and gateway.
pictures.caption: The main temple spaces form a connected architectural sequence.

pictures.alt: Octagonally arranged pillars and stone beams support concentric carved ceiling rings that step inward towards an ornamental central pendant.
pictures.caption: Concentric stone ceiling rings culminate in a carved central pendant.

title: Recognising a Solanki Temple: Plan, Tower, Pillars and Ornamentation

body:
Location, date and dedication

The Sun Temple at Modhera is one of the most important surviving monuments of the Solanki architectural tradition. It is located at Modhera in Mehsana district, Gujarat, near the Pushpavati River.

The temple is dedicated to Surya, the Sun. Its construction is generally dated to 1026–27 CE, during the reign of Bhima I of the Chaulukya or Solanki dynasty.

The monument demonstrates how a temple, an assembly hall and a ceremonial water tank could be organised as one architectural composition. Each part had a different role, but the whole complex was planned around a common axis.

The 3 principal components

The Modhera complex has 3 principal components: the stepped tank, the assembly hall and the main temple.

1. Surya Kund or Rama Kund

The Surya Kund, also called Rama Kund, is a large rectangular stepped water tank situated in front of the temple.

Its walls contain an elaborate pattern of steps descending towards the water. Small shrines are placed between the flights of steps. The tank is associated with 108 miniature shrines, a distinctive factual feature of the Modhera monument.

The tank demonstrates both the architectural importance of water and the ability of builders to organise numerous steps and shrines into a balanced geometric composition.

2. Sabha Mandapa

The Sabha Mandapa is the assembly hall situated between the tank and the main temple. It is an open-sided, richly ornamented pillared structure, distinct from the enclosed hall associated with the sanctum.

The pillars, beams and ornamental arches display intricate carving. A monumental torana formed part of the approach from the tank towards the assembly hall.

3. Main shrine and Gudhamandapa

Beyond the assembly hall is the principal temple structure. It includes the Gudhamandapa, or enclosed hall, and the garbhagriha, or inner sanctum.

Although parts of the original superstructure have been lost, the surviving walls and pillars reveal a sophisticated arrangement of architectural projections, carved niches and ornamentation. The complex is an important example of the development of Nagara architecture in western India.

Sunlight and the solar theme

The temple is oriented towards the east. Its arrangement is traditionally described as allowing the rays of the rising sun to reach the inner shrine at the equinoxes, when day and night are approximately equal in duration.

The temple's carvings also include representations of the 12 Adityas, associated with the 12 months of the year. These carvings emphasise its solar dedication.

The original sacred image no longer survives in the sanctum. Therefore, an explanation of the temple's original solar alignment should not be confused with a claim that the original image or all elements of the original building remain intact today.

108 miniature shrines belong to the stepped Surya Kund. 12 Aditya representations belong to the temple's solar iconography. These numbers refer to different features.

Why Modhera is architecturally important

Modhera combines several characteristic features of the Solanki style: a planned axial arrangement, ornamental entrance, open pillared assembly hall, enclosed temple hall, finely carved stone pillars and a monumental stepped tank.

The site also illustrates that temple architecture was not restricted to the shrine building alone. Movement through the tank area, ceremonial entrance and halls formed part of the overall experience of approaching the sanctum.

World Heritage classification

Modhera Sun Temple and its adjoining monuments were submitted to India's UNESCO Tentative List on 13 December 2022. A Tentative List entry is a proposal for potential future nomination and is not the same as inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

This must be distinguished from Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, which was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2014.

Prelims focus

  • Location: Modhera, Mehsana district, Gujarat, near the Pushpavati River.
  • Patronage and date: reign of Bhima I, 1026–27 CE.
  • Dedication: Surya, the Sun.
  • Principal parts: Surya Kund, Sabha Mandapa and main shrine with Gudhamandapa.
  • 108 miniature shrines occur in the stepped tank; 12 Adityas are associated with solar iconography.
  • Trap: Modhera's 2022 UNESCO Tentative List entry must not be confused with Rani-ki-Vav's 2014 World Heritage inscription.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 6, printed pp. 75–76; Krishna Deva, Temples of North India, 1969, chapter VI, printed pp. 45–46; Archaeological Survey of India, Newsletter, December 2022, section on Modhera Sun Temple; Gujarat Tourism, Modhera Sun Temple, consulted 23 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative Lists, Sun Temple, Modhera and its adjoining monuments, submission dated 13 December 2022, consulted 23 November 2026.]
